Abortion is not murder — here are the facts:
Murder is a legal term.
Murder is defined as the unlawful killing of a person with intent (malice aforethought). Abortion is a legal, medically regulated procedure performed with the consent of the pregnant person. By law, it does not meet the definition of murder in any jurisdiction where it’s permitted.
A fetus is not a legal person.
In U.S. law (and most global legal systems), personhood begins at birth, not conception. Until birth, a fetus is considered potential life, not a separate legal individual. The Supreme Court and medical consensus both distinguish between “human life” at a cellular level and “personhood” with rights.
Medical science defines pregnancy differently than anti-abortion rhetoric.
Pregnancy is the state in which an embryo or fetus develops inside the uterus, entirely dependent on the pregnant person’s body. Until the point of viability (roughly 23–24 weeks gestation), a fetus cannot survive independently, meaning it’s biologically part of the pregnant person — not a separate living entity.
Abortion is a medical intervention, not a violent act.
Most abortions occur before 12 weeks, when the embryo or fetus has no brain activity, nervous system function, or consciousness. There is no capacity for awareness, pain, or suffering. It’s a clinical, ethical healthcare procedure, often necessary to preserve the health, fertility, or life of the patient.
Criminalizing abortion increases death, not life.
According to the World Health Organization, countries that ban abortion have similar rates of abortion — but far higher rates of maternal death and injury.
